source_document.body:
Photo: © Roza | Dreamstime.com
By Keith Mwanalushi
27 November 2026
Alaska Air Group is doubling its dedicated freighter fleet as it looks to unlock cargo demand in Hawaii and build a more substantial international freight business.
However, the challenge might be turning that additional aircraft capacity into sustainable revenue growth.
The airline plans to introduce four Boeing 737-800 converted freighters in the first half of next year, increasing its dedicated narrowbody fleet from five to nine aircraft.
Two are earmarked for Alaska Airlines and two for sister carrier Hawaiian Airlines, with the flexibility to allocate capacity across the network according to demand and operational needs.
Each aircraft can carry approximately 50,000lb of cargo, giving the carriers greater scope to develop regional freight operations while connecting shipments with its expanding international network.
For Hawaii, the investment addresses what Alaska describes as an existing capacity constraint. Hawaiian Airlines has served the market for nearly 85 years, but its reliance on passenger aircraft has limited its ability to meet the full potential of the cargo market, according to Ian Morgan, VP cargo at Alaska Airlines.
“By adding dedicated freighter service and leveraging Hawaiian’s brand, we can meet that demand while empowering a more interconnected, global network,” he told The Loadstar .
The new aircraft in Hawaii will support shipments between the islands and provide additional capacity for seafood, agricultural produce, and other locally manufactured goods.
Mr Morgan said the combined operations would help support local industries, particularly those requiring reliable, palletised transport, adding: “The freighter network will connect seamlessly with our widebody fleet,” he said.
The ability to move shipments under a single air waybill could give Hawaiian cargo customers greater access to international markets, although the commercial benefits will depend on the availability of onward capacity, competitive transit times, and the ability to attract sufficient freight volumes.
The opportunity is significant, given the geographical challenges of serving Hawaii’s dispersed island communities. Dedicated aircraft could provide greater consistency for larger shipments, while passenger aircraft continue to offer additional belly capacity.
The expansion also comes as Alaska Air Group seeks to make cargo a more significant contributor to its overall business. Its Alaska Accelerate strategy identifies cargo as an important source of revenue diversification. Alaska’s growth opportunities span cargo services in Alaska and Hawaii, the continental US, international operations, ACMI leasing, and other ancillary engagements, according to Mr Morgan.
The group has set a target of growing annual cargo revenue to $750m by 2030, having increased cargo revenue by approximately 60% since 2024, according to its September investor day presentation. Opportunities also include mail, international belly capacity, and broader network connectivity.
Beyond its own network, the reference to ACMI leasing – providing aircraft, crews, maintenance, and insurance to third-party operators – could allow Alaska to generate additional returns from its freighter assets, although the airline has not detailed how much of its future fleet capacity might be allocated to such arrangements.
Mr Morgan said the objective was to reach new markets while maintaining the reliability of existing services.
“Doubling our dedicated freighter capacity gives us more room to pursue opportunities in Alaska and Hawaiʻi, while giving us more flexibility to allocate aircraft where they are needed,” he added.
The challenge is ensuring the additional capacity attracts new cargo business rather than simply shifting existing volumes between more aircraft. Ultimately, Alaska’s success may rest on how effectively it connects regional markets to its expanding international network.

source_document.body:
Storage
Kioxia GP2 Series SSDs
Kioxia is introducing the GP2 Series SSD, and the standout number is more than 18 million random read IOPS at a 512-byte block size. I think we actually saw a precursor to this drive a few weeks ago. 18M IOPS is nearly double the performance of the GP1 Series Kioxia showed in August at FMS. The new drive is designed for PCIe 6.0 and NVMe 2.3, and Kioxia says it is also expecting sequential read throughput of up to 28GB/s, enough to saturate a PCIe 6.0 x4 link.
Kioxia GP2 Series Launched
The GP series is designed for a specific role in AI systems. Instead of adding more expensive HBM or DRAM to a GPU system, operators can use these NAND-based drives to create a flash-based memory tier the GPU can access directly. This lets the system handle larger datasets at a lower cost. Whenever you try to replace DRAM with NAND, endurance becomes a question. At 50DWPD, the GP2 is a step above many of the common capacity-focused drives.
 | Kioxia GP2 Series
Interface | PCIe 6.0 / NVMe 2.3
Flash Memory | Kioxia XL-FLASH generation 3
Random Read Performance | More than 18 million IOPS at 512-byte block size
Expected Sequential Read Throughput | Up to 28 GB/s
Endurance | Up to 50 DWPD
Form Factors Under Consideration | E1.S 9.5 mm and E3.S
Cooling | Direct liquid cooling support
Kioxia is using its XL-FLASH generation 3 memory in the GP2. The company says this low-latency flash is better suited for the fine-grained data access needed for memory expansion than typical TLC-based SSDs. Kioxia also claims XL-FLASH generation 3 provides higher endurance and about 2.5x the IOPS of its own TLC-based CM10 Series SSDs at a 512-byte block size.
Kioxia GP Series SSD preview at OCP Summit 2026
Kioxia previewed its next-generation GP series at OCP Summit 2026 in the demo above, with a 20M IOPS system running live. The company says future generations will target up to 100 million random read IOPS, but we are not there just yet.
Final Words
Kioxia says evaluation GP2 samples will be available to select customers by the end of 2027, so this seems a bit further out. We are starting to see more PCIe Gen6 systems, as you may have seen in our recent AMD EPYC 9006 Results Are Here and AMD Delivers a Knockout Part Deux piece, where we had both AMD and NVIDIA PCIe Gen6 systems. Hopefully, we will get to try these out when they ship.
Of course, happy Thanksgiving to those in the US.

Amazon’s Black Friday Week started on November 19, but the main event goes live on Black Friday, November 27, 2026.

Technically speaking Amazon’s Black Friday sale runs through November 27 before it transitions into a Cyber Monday weekend sale, but the deals will run right through Monday, November 30.

Sometimes yes, sometimes no. Retailers, Amazon included, have become incredibly aggressive with early discounts and often deliver the best deals of the season on select items well ahead of Black Friday. That’s, however, not always the case and some gear will drop lower as the sale progresses.
What time does the Amazon Black Friday sale start?
The official Amazon Black Friday main event sale begins at 3:00 a.m. ET on November 27, 2026.
What time does the Amazon Black Friday sale end?
The official Amazon Black Friday main event sale ends at 11:59 p.m. PT on November 27, 2026/2:59 a.m. ET on November 28.

source_document.body:
Volvo flew us out to Copenhagen to drive across the bridge to Sweden to check out the upcoming 2028 XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. The new vehicles promise to double the EV-only range to 73-78 miles, making them a new breed of hybrid rarely seen outside China. But what can you do with so much EV-only range?
At Electrek , we’re usually pretty skeptical of plug-in hybrids. Too many are glorified gas cars with 20-mile batteries that owners often don’t bother to charge. The electric-only powertrain is often underpowered and not something you can actually use day-to-day.
Volvo’s upcoming 2028 XC60 T8 and XC90 T8 “Long-Range” PHEVs are the rare exception that actually force us to pay attention. By stuffing a 41.2 kWh floor-mounted battery (37.9 kWh usable) into its solid but aging SPA1 platform, Volvo has more than doubled the electric range of its two bestselling SUVs. Both now have more battery capacity and range than the original all-electric Nissan Leaf, Hyundai Ioniq, and many of the compliance EVs that followed. Volvo also doubled the charging speed from 3.6kW to a more reasonable 7.2 kW, meaning charge times are roughly unchanged.
The Powertrain: Finally enough battery to matter
Both the XC60 and XC90 share the exact same T8 AWD hardware: a 247-hp 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder up front with a 70-hp front e-boost motor, and an upgraded 174-hp electric motor on the rear axle. Combined output lands at a healthy 455 horsepower and 560 lb-ft of torque .
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The real headline, though, is the electric range:
2028 XC60 T8: Up to 78 miles of preliminary EPA-estimated EV range (590 miles combined) and 67 MPGe .
2028 XC90 T8: Up to 73 miles of preliminary EPA-estimated EV range and 61 MPGe .
Those numbers easily crown both Volvos as the longest-range plug-in hybrids coming to the U.S. market, blowing past the Mercedes-Benz GLE 450e, Toyota RAV4 Prime, and Range Rover PHEVs, which top out around 50 miles. With the average American commuting around 30 to 40 miles a day, you can genuinely treat either of these SUVs like a full EV Monday through Friday without waking up the gas engine once…or so it would appear on paper.
Sadly, there are some caveats to consider that will make these a little harder to run EV-only. First, to accelerate quickly off the line or to operate in AWD mode, the gas engine needs to engage. That makes winter driving and spirited driving a gas-usage endeavor. Also, without DC fast charging, the Level 2 charger tops out at 7.2 kW, meaning longer trips will also require gas usage.
On the plus side, even with the cold weather and snow tires, I saw range over 145 kilometers/90 miles on the XC60 when fully charged.
2028 Volvo XC60 T8: The sharper, fresher pick
If you don’t need a third row, the XC60 is easily the more compelling package.
At 4,855 lbs, it’s quick—ripping from 0–60 mph in 4.5 seconds —and surprisingly efficient for a bulky crossover, sipping 48 kWh per 100 miles in electric mode and returning 29 mpg combined once the battery is depleted. Unlike the XC90, the 2028 XC60 also gets a proper visual refresh, complete with a cleaner front fascia, Matrix LED headlights, horizontal taillights, and an updated interior featuring Google Gemini on its not huge but very usable 11.2-inch touchscreen.
It’s also the easier daily driver in tight spaces, with a 37.4-foot turning circle and slightly more first- and second-row legroom than its bigger sibling . The trade-off is utility: you’re limited to 21.1 cu. ft. of cargo space behind the second row and a 3,500-lb towing capacity .
2028 Volvo XC90 T8: The three-row bridge to full EVs
The XC90 is the family hauler for buyers who want a three-row electric SUV but aren’t quite ready to jump into an EX90 or Rivian R1S.
Because Volvo redesigned the battery into a flat, floor-mounted pack, you don’t lose the XC90’s practicality . You still get 6- or 7-passenger seating, 34.5 cu. ft. of cargo room behind the second row (up to 69.4 cu. ft. max), and a serious 5,000-lb towing rating . Even with the extra bulk, it hits 60 mph in 4.9 seconds .
The downside? Efficiency drops to 53 kWh per 100 miles (27 mpg on gas), the third row’s 31.9 inches of legroom is still best reserved for kids, and outside of the new battery and Google Gemini integration, the cabin and exterior are essentially carryovers, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing since we love Volvo interiors.
The big EV caveats:
Even with a 41.2 kWh pack, you can’t completely hide the compromises of a plug-in hybrid:
No fast charging in sight: Refilling that 37.9 kWh usable pack takes 5.7 hours on a standard U.S. Level 2 home charger—and a painful 27 to 53 hours on a regular 120V wall outlet. I don’t hate this because on trips and other times that you need quick range, you’ll just jump into gas mode, but it would be nice to have DC fast charging
RWD-only in EV mode: Because the gas engine (plus an EV helper motor that can’t operate on its own) powers the front wheels and the main electric motor drives the rear, running in pure EV mode means you’re driving a rear-wheel-drive SUV. In winter weather, demanding all-wheel-drive traction forces the gas engine to kick on. So does gunning it at a green light and the motor stays on for a bit.
Double the complexity: You’re still maintaining an 18-gallon fuel tank, a turbocharged four-cylinder, and an 8-speed automatic transmission alongside a full EV battery pack. More to haul around, more space taken up and more to go wrong.
Not a direct EV issue but the Volvo SP1 doesn’t do wireless Carplay/Android Auto natively. You’ll need to plug into USB-C or buy a third party dongle to connect wirelessly. The upside is that Google’s Android in Volvo center stack has most of the same apps as your phone and a fast, native display vs the lag sometimes felt in projection systems.
Electrek’s Take
Look, we’d still rather see buyers go all-electric with the upcoming EX60 or EX90, and if Volvo prices these 2028 T8s too close to $70,000–$80,000 when deliveries start in early 2027, going full BEV will still be a no-brainer in my book.
But for those who aren’t ready to make the leap to full EV, these vehicles are incredibly compelling. Every morning, assuming you’re on a Level 2 charger, you have almost 80 miles of EV range, about double the average American daily usage. Then, of course, the backup of the 18-gallon tank and gas motor for those edge cases like trips or towing in cold weather are covered.
So the takeaway: if you’re going to build a plug-in hybrid in 2027, this is how you do it. Giving drivers 73 to 78 miles of real electric range turns the gas engine from a daily necessity into a road-trip range extender. For households with a Level 2 home charger that still have lingering charging anxiety on long highway trips, the 2028 XC60 and XC90 T8 are easily the smartest PHEVs on the market. Not to mention the smooth, quick and safe rides Volvo is known for.
